AttnFuse: A Composable DSL for Compiling Attentions to Fused GPU Kernels

Varun Kumar Dasoju Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Email: dasoju@uwm.edu    Tian Zhao Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Email: tzhao@uwm.edu
Abstract

Modern AI systems are built on the Transformer architecture, whose core operation, attention, accounts for the majority of computation and memory cost. Researchers continually propose new attention variants to improve quality, efficiency, or context length, but each variant currently requires expert-written GPU code to run at usable speeds. PyTorch’s recent flex_attention lets researchers describe custom attention patterns in Python and compile them to fused kernels, but its design is limited to modifications applied after the central matrix multiplication, excluding Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), the positional encoding used by every major LLM.

We introduce AttnFuse, a small DSL for attention that makes pre-multiplication transformations like RoPE first-class operations. Researchers compose ten high-level building blocks to describe a variant, and AttnFuse’s compiler emits a single fused GPU kernel for the entire computation. On an RTX 3090, AttnFuse achieves a 2.10×\times speedup over flex_attention on the RoPE+causal pattern. On an H100, it runs a full Llama-3-8B training step within 5% of PyTorch’s hand-tuned backend. Our investigation reveals the Rotation Calculus: whether to fuse RoPE or apply it separately depends on the GPU’s compute-to-bandwidth ratio, with a derived crossover that matches measurement. AttnFuse demonstrates that a small, attention-specific compiler can close the gap between flexible research code and production kernels.

   

A Preprint

1 Introduction

The attention bottleneck.

At the heart of every modern language model lies a single operation called attention. Given a sequence of tokens, attention computes which prior tokens are most relevant to each new token, then aggregates their information. This operation accounts for the majority of both computation and memory cost in models like ChatGPT, Claude, and LLaMA. Making attention faster is therefore one of the central problems in AI systems research.

The challenge is that attention is memory-intensive. On a GPU, moving data between slow off-chip memory and fast on-chip memory is expensive. Naive implementations write the full intermediate score matrix to off-chip memory, which becomes prohibitive at long sequence lengths. Kernel fusion solves this by combining operations into a single GPU program that keeps intermediate values on-chip, dramatically reducing memory traffic. FlashAttention [1, 2] is the canonical fused kernel: a hand-written CUDA program that underpins nearly every production LLM today. But it is fixed and inflexible.

The researcher’s dilemma.

AI researchers constantly invent new attention variants – sliding windows [6], linear biases [7], sparse patterns, and more – to improve quality, efficiency, or context length. Each new variant currently requires expert-written GPU code to run at useful speeds. This creates a persistent gap: high-level Python code is flexible but slow, while production kernels like FlashAttention are fast but inflexible.

PyTorch 2.5 introduced flex_attention [14], a promising step toward bridging this gap. Researchers write a small Python function that modifies attention scores, and a compiler turns it into a fused GPU kernel via Triton [4, 17]. flex_attention is the strongest published bridge between researcher convenience and production performance, supporting sliding windows, ALiBi, and arbitrary score modifications.

A fundamental limitation.

flex_attention has one important limitation: its modification function operates on the score matrix after the multiplication Q​K⊤QK^{\top}. Many useful attention variants require transformations before this multiplication. The most consequential example is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [8] – the position encoding used by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and every other recent major LLM. RoPE rotates queries and keys before multiplication, encoding position information in the geometry of the vectors themselves. Because the rotation applies to QQ and KK separately, it cannot be expressed as a post-matmul score modification. The current workaround applies RoPE in a separate kernel before calling flex_attention, paying two extra memory round-trips per attention layer (Figure 1a).

AttnFuse is a domain-specific language (DSL) for attention that makes pre-multiplication transformations first-class operations. Researchers compose ten high-level building blocks to describe an attention variant declaratively – for example, softmax(causal(rope(Q, K))) @ V. AttnFuse’s compiler then emits a single fused GPU kernel for the entire program. This is a strictly more general abstraction that includes pre-matmul fusions by construction.

Contributions.

We make three contributions:

  • •

    A compilable DSL for attention. A ten-combinator DSL with a two-level IR and four-pass compiler guaranteeing single-kernel fusion for any well-formed program.

  • •

    Fused RoPE. Pre-matmul fusion of RoPE into attention inner loop, achieving 2.10×2.10\times over flex_attention on causal+RoPE at N=4096N=4096 on RTX 3090.

  • •

    The Rotation Calculus. A quantitative principle linking fusion profitability to compute-to-bandwidth ratio: fusion wins on Ampere; crossover at N∗≈5,500N^{*}\approx 5{,}500 on Hopper, derived algebraically and confirmed experimentally.

The paper also presents a complete engineering artifact –Flash Decoding, backward pass, block-sparse attention, HuggingFace integration, and a documented Triton limitation – validating the DSL on real workloads, including Llama-3-8B training within 5% of PyTorch’s hand-tuned backend on H100.

2 Background

FlashAttention and online softmax.

FlashAttention [1, 2] introduced a key algorithmic insight: the softmax normalization [5] can be computed incrementally, tile by tile, without materializing the full N×NN\times N score matrix. The algorithm maintains a running max mm, a running sum ℓ\ell, and a partial output accumulator across tiles of keys. When a new tile arrives, the running state is rescaled to account for any change in the maximum. This recurrence is exact and reduces the number of off-chip memory accesses from 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) to 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) per query row. In online softmax, the running state (m,ℓ,acc)(m,\ell,\text{acc}) lives entirely in GPU registers, so the full score matrix is never written to off-chip memory. This is the foundation of efficient attention implementation.

Why fusion is not always profitable.

Fusing operations saves off-chip memory traffic but often increases the amount of computation performed on-chip. Whether a fusion is profitable depends on the GPU’s balance between compute throughput and memory bandwidth. This balance is captured by the roofline model: a kernel’s performance is limited by whichever resource is the bottleneck.

Triton.

Triton [4] is a language for writing GPU kernels at a tile level, higher-level than raw CUDA but lower-level than PyTorch. It compiles to GPU machine code through an MLIR-based backend. AttnFuse generates Triton code; we do not modify the Triton compiler itself, though we identify a lowering limitation in version 3.3.1 that creates a useful negative result (Section 7.2).

Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE).

RoPE [8] encodes position by rotating each pair of dimensions in QQ and KK by an angle proportional to token position, making the dot product ⟨Qi′,Kj′⟩\langle Q^{\prime}_{i},K^{\prime}_{j}\rangle depend only on relative position j−ij-i. Because the rotation applies to QQ and KK separately before Q​K⊤QK^{\top}, RoPE is a pre-matmul transformation and therefore impossible to express in flex_attention’s post-matmul score_mod (Figure 1).

3 System Design

AttnFuse is designed for AI researchers to implement new attention variants in Python and get a fused GPU kernel that matches production performance. Figure 2 shows the four-layer pipeline. The user writes a function using ten composable building blocks; AttnFuse traces the function once per configuration, compiles it through four passes, and dispatches the compiled kernel at runtime with negligible overhead.

3.1 The Researcher Interface

AttnFuse exposes ten combinators that correspond to common attention operations: scaled_dot_product, rope, causal, sliding_window, full, block_sparse, alibi, additive_bias, softmax, and relu_attention. A researcher defines an attention variant by composing these combinators:

⬇
@af.attention
def llama_attn(Q, K, V):
s = af.rope(Q, K) # RoPE applied before matmul
s = af.causal(s) # causal mask
return af.softmax(s) @ V # softmax & value aggregation

The @af.attention decorator traces this function once, capturing the computation graph. The DSL is intentionally narrow: it cannot express flex_attention’s arbitrary score_mod callback. This is by design – the narrowness is what lets AttnFuse guarantee that every well-formed program compiles to a single fused kernel. Adding a new combinator like rope() requires defining its semantics and its compiler effect, but this is a one-time effort; researchers using the DSL never touch the compiler.

3.2 From DSL to Kernel

The compiler transforms the user’s computation graph through four passes and two intermediate representation (IR):

  1. 1.

    Fuse: Recognizes the canonical attention pattern – score computation, masking, normalization, and value aggregation – and verifies that the graph is fusible.

  2. 2.

    Tile: Selects tile sizes (block dimensions, number of warps, pipeline stages) appropriate for the target GPU architecture and attention variant. Tuning tables are precomputed from the sweeps described in Section 5.2.

  3. 3.

    Lower: Converts the graph to a flat TiledKernel record with all constants needed for code generation.

  4. 4.

    Codegen: Emits Triton source. The generated kernel has no runtime branching, all variant-specific logic is resolved at compile time via Triton’s constexpr mechanism.

The high-level IR uses six node types: TensorSym for input tensors, ScoreOp for score computation, MaskOp and BiasOp for modifications, NormOp for softmax variants, and MatMulPV for the final value aggregation. Each graph carries a SHA-1 signature over its structural content, which serves as a cache key for compiled kernels. The low-level IR captures tile shapes, architecture-specific flags, and constants like ROPE_KIND, MASK_KIND, and SAVE_L.

3.3 Runtime Dispatch

At runtime, run_attention() computes the graph’s signature, looks up a precompiled LaunchBundle, and invokes the kernel. Three fast paths bypass the general kernel:

  • •

    Flash Decoding: When the query batch size is 1 (autoregressive inference), the KV cache is split across multiple programs for better parallelism (Section 4.2).

  • •

    Block-sparse: When a sparse block mask is supplied, the kernel iterates only over active blocks (Section 4.3).

  • •

    Hopper spike: On H100 GPUs, a tile-swept kernel variant is used for causal attention (Section 5.2).

Steady-state dispatch overhead is under 1​μ1\,\mus, so the runtime cost is negligible relative to the kernel execution time.

4 Key Optimizations

This section describes four optimizations that demonstrate AttnFuse’s expressiveness and performance.

4.1 Fused RoPE

When a researcher includes rope(Q, K) in their DSL program, AttnFuse’s code generator produces a kernel that rotates the query matrix once, before the outer loop, and rotates each key tile on the fly inside the inner loop. The rotation follows the standard NeoX convention: each pair of dimensions is rotated by an angle that depends on the token’s position. This is implemented using a precomputed index offset and sign multiplier to access the rotated half of each vector.

4.2 Flash Decoding

For autoregressive decoding, the query batch size is 1. The standard FlashAttention-2 kernel launches only B⋅HqB\cdot H_{q} programs (e.g., 32 for Llama-3-8B), which underutilizes modern GPUs with hundreds of streaming multiprocessors.

AttnFuse’s Flash Decoding path addresses this by splitting the KV cache across multiple programs. Phase 1 launches one program per chunk of the KV cache; each program computes a partial (m,ℓ,acc)(m,\ell,\text{acc}) triple using the online-softmax loop. Phase 2 runs a small combine kernel that merges these partials via log-sum-exp to produce the final output. For models using Grouped-Query Attention, we pad the number of query heads per program to 16 by cyclic replication, loading KK and VV exactly once per program while recovering full tensor-core throughput. On Llama-3-70B with a 32k cache, this optimization reduces latency from 3,153​μ3{,}153\,\mus to 184​μ184\,\mus—a 17×17\times speedup, beating flex_attention’s 196​μ196\,\mus.

4.3 Block-Sparse Attention

Many efficient attention variants use sparse masks to reduce quadratic complexity. AttnFuse supports block-sparse attention: the user supplies a Python predicate over block coordinates; create_block_mask evaluates it once and returns a CSR-style BlockMask with per-row active-block index lists. Both forward and backward kernels iterate only over active blocks, producing genuinely sub-quadratic FLOPs.

On the BigBird mask [9] at N=4096N{=}4096 (∼7.7%\sim 7.7\% active blocks), AttnFuse forward runs at 84​μ84\,\mus vs. flex_attention’s 270​μ270\,\mus, a 3.21×3.21\times speedup. The advantage is structural: flex_attention pays full 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) FLOPs and masks inactive tiles to −∞-\infty, while AttnFuse pays proportionally to the active fraction.

4.4 Backward Pass

AttnFuse implements a full backward pass following the FlashAttention-2 design. The backward decomposes into three kernels: a preprocessing kernel that computes row-reduced gradients, a kernel that accumulates gradients with respect to keys and values, and a kernel that accumulates gradients with respect to queries. This split avoids atomic accumulation: each kernel writes to a clean per-program output tile. The forward pass saves a single scalar per query row (L=m+log⁡ℓL=m+\log\ell), which is sufficient to re-derive softmax probabilities tile-by-tile during the backward pass without ever materializing the full score matrix.

5 A Cross-Architecture Analysis

The previous sections established that AttnFuse can express and fuse RoPE. But is fusion always the right choice? This section shows that the answer depends on the hardware. We report a structured investigation on H100 NVL (sm_90) that begins with a porting failure, proceeds through systematic tuning, and culminates in a general principle we call the Rotation Calculus: whether fused RoPE beats pre-rotation is determined by the GPU’s compute-to-bandwidth ratio.

5.1 The Hopper Gap

Porting the Ampere-kernel template to H100 NVL produces a 2.10×2.10\times slowdown vs. flex_attention on causal forward at N=4096N{=}4096. We profiled both kernels with Nsight Compute; Table 1 reports the counter triangulation. The production kernel also shows higher register pressure (217 vs. 255 regs/thread) and lower shared memory usage (65 vs. 113 KB/block), consistent with its less aggressive tiling.

A key reframing emerges from these numbers: flex_attention’s HMMA pipe sits at 32.6%32.6\% on H100, not the 6060–70%70\% that CUTLASS-class Hopper kernels reach. The FA-2 algorithm at this shape is structurally bounded by its non-matmul fraction (online softmax, mask logic, address arithmetic); even fully optimized codegen cannot meaningfully exceed ∼35%\sim 35\% HMMA. This reframes the Hopper goal from “WGMMA codegen needed” to “match flex’s ceiling, then look for algorithm-level gains.”

5.2 Sweep-Tuning for Hopper

We executed a 16-configuration sweep over num_stages∈{2,3,4}\text{num\_stages}\in\{2,3,4\}, BLOCK_N∈{64,128,256}\text{BLOCK\_N}\in\{64,128,256\}, and num_warps∈{4,8}\text{num\_warps}\in\{4,8\} with BLOCK_M=128\text{BLOCK\_M}{=}128 fixed. Table 2 summarizes the results.

Three findings generalize:

  1. 1.

    The sparse-table heuristic inverts on Hopper. On Ampere, causal variants want BN=32\text{BN}{=}32 for more programs per SM. On Hopper, the winner is BN=64\text{BN}{=}64 for plain causal and BN=128\text{BN}{=}128 for RoPE+causal.

  2. 2.

    num_warps=8\text{num\_warps}{=}8 strictly dominates. num_warps=4\text{num\_warps}{=}4 is 22–3×3\times slower in all sweep entries. Hopper wants one full warp-group per program.

  3. 3.

    num_stages=3\text{num\_stages}{=}3 vs. 4 is essentially flat. Pipeline depth matters less than getting the matmul shape right.

The sweep-tuned kernel is packaged as a dispatch-time fast path (Table 3) that activates on H100 for causal attention, closing 85%85\% of the gap to flex_attention via tile selection alone.

5.3 The Rotation Calculus

We now extend the spike to fused RoPE+causal and measure the cross-architecture comparison. These measurements reveal a general principle: the Rotation Calculus. Whether to fuse RoPE inside the attention kernel or pre-rotate QQ and KK separately is determined by the platform’s compute-to-bandwidth ratio. Pre-rotation pays an 𝒪⁡(N​H​D)\mathcal{O}(NHD) HBM round-trip once; in-kernel fusion pays an 𝒪⁡(N2​D/BM)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}D/\text{BM}) rotation cost inside the FA-2 causal loop. On a bandwidth-bound platform (Ampere, ≈152\approx 152 FLOPs/byte ridge), fusion wins decisively. On a compute-rich platform (Hopper, ≈300\approx 300 FLOPs/byte ridge), the crossover occurs between N=4​kN{=}4\text{k} and N=8​kN{=}8\text{k}. Table 4 shows the headline result.

Algebraic identification of the crossover.

The pre-rotation cost is Tpre=4​B​H​N​D⋅2/BWT_{\text{pre}}=4BHND\cdot 2/\text{BW} seconds (read Q,KQ,K, write Q′,K′Q^{\prime},K^{\prime}). The in-kernel rotation cost is Tfused≈Ntiles⋅crotT_{\text{fused}}\approx N_{\text{tiles}}\cdot c_{\text{rot}} where Ntiles=B​H​N2/(BM⋅BN)N_{\text{tiles}}=BHN^{2}/(\text{BM}\cdot\text{BN}) and crotc_{\text{rot}} is the per-tile rotation cost in cycles (∼800\sim 800 cycles on Hopper). Setting Tpre=TfusedT_{\text{pre}}=T_{\text{fused}} yields:

N∗≈8​D⋅BM⋅BN⋅FLOPSBW⋅crot.N^{*}\approx\sqrt{\frac{8D\cdot\text{BM}\cdot\text{BN}\cdot\text{FLOPS}}{\text{BW}\cdot c_{\text{rot}}}}. (1)

Plugging in H100 NVL numbers [16] (BW=3.9\text{BW}=3.9 TB/s, FLOPS=1015\text{FLOPS}=10^{15}, BM=128\text{BM}=128, BN=128\text{BN}=128, D=64D=64, crot=800c_{\text{rot}}=800) gives N∗≈6000N^{*}\approx 6000, consistent with the measured crossover between 4k and 8k.

5.4 Nsight Compute Profile of the RoPE Spike

To characterize where the in-kernel rotation cost goes on H100, we profiled the RoPE+causal spike against the plain-causal spike (Table 5). The diagnostic combination is long-scoreboard rising 5.5×5.5\times while DRAM utilization decreases: many small HBM-latency-blocked loads (cos, sin, Krot_halfK_{\text{rot\_half}}) without bandwidth saturation. This motivated a targeted optimization attempt (documented in Section 7.2).

6 Evaluation

All measurements use PyTorch 2.5.1, CUDA 12.1, Triton 3.1.0 (Ampere) or 3.3.1 (Hopper). Latency is the median of 40–50 CUDA-event-timed launches after 8–12 warmups. Evaluation hardware: RTX 3090 (sm_86, 24 GB GDDR6X, 82 SMs, 142 TFLOPS fp16 peak); H100 NVL (sm_90, 132 SMs, ∼\sim1000 TFLOPS fp16 peak via WGMMA). Three baselines: naive (PyTorch eager-mode), sdpa (torch.nn.functional. scaled_dot_product_attention), and flex_attention (PyTorch 2.5’s compiled attention).

6.1 Forward Head-to-Head on Ampere

Table 6 reports AttnFuse vs. flex_attention on GPT-2-small geometry (B=4,H=12,D=64B{=}4,H{=}12,D{=}64) in fp16. Cells show speedup =flex/AttnFuse=\text{flex}/\text{AttnFuse} (bold == AttnFuse wins). AttnFuse wins 12 of 16 cells, with sliding-window attention showing a clean sweep.

6.2 RoPE on Ampere

Because flex_attention’s score_mod is a post-matmul hook by design (Section 4.1), it applies RoPE host-side in two extra kernels. Table 7 reports the resulting speedup. AttnFuse wins every cell at 1.651.65–2.10×2.10\times.

6.3 KV-Cache Decoding

Table 8 reports AttnFuse Flash Decoding vs. flex_attention on three production LLM geometries with Q.N=1Q.N{=}1. The Llama-3-70B cell shows the 17×17\times improvement over the unsplit AttnFuse kernel.

6.4 H100 Causal Ablation

The H100 spike ablation (Table 3) shows the progression from the production Ampere-tuned kernel (0.9310.931 ms) through the FA-2 causal split (0.6940.694 ms) to the sweep-tuned winner (0.4880.488 ms), closing 85%85\% of the gap to flex_attention’s 0.4430.443 ms reference. The attempted half-swap optimization regressed to 0.9520.952 ms and was reverted (discussed in Section 7).

6.5 End-to-End: Llama-3-8B

To validate AttnFuse on a production workload, we benchmark a single Llama-3-8B LlamaDecoderLayer (random-init weights, Hq=32H_{q}{=}32, Hk​v=8H_{kv}{=}8, D=128D{=}128) with the HuggingFace transformers [15] integration. AttnFuse registers as an attn_implementation backend; switching is a one-line configuration change.

Table 9 reports latencies on H100 NVL. Forward-only, AttnFuse is essentially tied with PyTorch’s SDPA backend at N=2048N{=}2048, trailing by only 51​μ51\,\mus (+1.8%+1.8\%), and remains within 8%8\% at N=4096N{=}4096. For the full training step (forward, backward, and optimizer step), AttnFuse is within 5.2%5.2\% of SDPA at N=2048N{=}2048 and within 14.7%14.7\% at N=4096N{=}4096.

On RTX 3090, AttnFuse achieves 1.06×1.06\times SDPA on the training step; flex_attention OOMs at HEAD_DIM=128, so AttnFuse is the only Triton-based attention compiler that runs Llama-3-8B training on consumer Ampere. These results demonstrate that a DSL-emitted kernel can match hand-tuned CUDA on production workloads.

Two notes on the H100 numbers.

First, HuggingFace’s LlamaDecoderLayer applies RoPE to QQ and KK before calling the registered attention function, so the graph traced is plain causal, not fused RoPE. Threading cos\cos, sin\sin through the HF hook would invoke the fused-RoPE path, which per the Rotation Calculus should improve the forward number at N≤4​kN\leq 4\text{k}. Second, the spike’s dispatch predicate rejects calls with save_lse set, so the training-step forward uses the production kernel; widening predicate coverage would close the training-step gap. Both are well-scoped follow-on items.

6.6 Correctness

87 GPU pytest cells cover the variant matrix ×\times dtype ×\times shape ×\times GQA configuration. 80 Hypothesis-driven [11] property fuzzer examples randomize configurations across forward and backward. All gradients are verified against a naive PyTorch reference within FA2’s documented fp16 tolerance (|e​r​r|<2×10−2|err|<2\times 10^{-2}).

7 Discussion

The results reframe three common assumptions about attention codegen for modern GPUs and provide practical guidance for researchers and practitioners.

Hopper does not necessarily require WGMMA intrinsics for attention.

Section 5 measured flex_attention’s HMMA pipe ceiling on H100 at 32.6%32.6\%, not the 6060–70%70\% that CUTLASS-class Hopper kernels sometimes reach. The FA-2 non-matmul fraction – online softmax, mask logic, address arithmetic – is the binding constraint at this shape, not the WGMMA-vs-HMMA codegen choice. Our sweep-tuned spike reaches 29.4%29.4\% HMMA via tile selection alone, within 3.23.2 percentage points of this ceiling. Closing the residual gap requires FA-3-style algorithmic restructure (producer/consumer warp specialization that overlaps softmax with the next matmul), not explicit Hopper intrinsics. For AI systems researchers, this means that significant Hopper gains for attention may come from algorithm redesign rather than low-level tuning alone.

Fusion is platform-dependent, and that’s quantifiable.

The Rotation Calculus is the explicit form of an intuition the FlashAttention community has long gestured at: as accelerators rebalance toward compute, the value of HBM-saving fusions shrinks. We measure and quantify the crossover for fused RoPE; the same algebra applies to any pre-matmul fusion whose in-kernel cost grows with NN faster than its pre-pass analogue. For practitioners, this provides a concrete rule: on compute-rich hardware like H100, pre-rotation may be preferable for long contexts; on bandwidth-bound hardware like Ampere, fusion is almost always the right choice.

A high-level DSL can match hand-tuned CUDA on production LLMs.

The 51​μ51\,\mus gap from SDPA at N=2048N{=}2048 forward on H100, and the 5%5\% training-step gap at the same shape, are the production-grade claim. The DSL surface is what makes adding the next variant a one-day change rather than a multi-week kernel rewrite. This suggests that the historical tradeoff between researcher productivity and production performance is not fundamental; attention-specific compilation can offer both.

7.1 Workload Positioning

Where is AttnFuse the right choice today? Based on our results, AttnFuse is the strong choice for LLM fine-tuning at 22k–44k tokens (within 5%5\% of SDPA on training, 2.10×2.10\times over flex_attention on RTX 3090 for RoPE), KV-cache inference at 44k–3232k cache lengths (17×17\times speedup over unsplit AttnFuse, parity with flex_attention on Llama-3-70B at 32k), and block-sparse training (3.21×3.21\times over flex_attention on BigBird at N=4N{=}4k). It is comparable to flex_attention on ALiBi, sliding window, and custom score modifications (55–10%10\% range on Ampere), where the DSL surface is the primary value. Long-context RoPE on Hopper (N≥16N\geq 16k) is future work: the Rotation Calculus favors pre-rotation at these lengths, and an FA-3-style producer/consumer kernel is the path forward. For full pre-training at 44k–88k, the picture is mixed: forward parity on H100, but the backward uses the production kernel (spike predicate rejects save_lse-set calls), and RoPE crosses over near N≈6N\approx 6k.

7.2 Lessons Learned: A Negative Result

The investigation of fused RoPE on Hopper revealed a compiler limitation worth documenting. The NCU diagnosis of the RoPE spike (Section 5) pointed at the per-tile Krot_halfK_{\text{rot\_half}} HBM load as the dominant new stall: long-scoreboard stalls rose 5.5×5.5\times from 3.1%3.1\% to 17.5%17.5\%, while DRAM utilization actually decreased. The Krot_halfK_{\text{rot\_half}} tile is KK with the two DD-halves swapped; algebraically, it can be derived from KK by a register layout permutation with no second HBM access.

We implemented this via Triton’s tl.reshape + tl.permute + tl.split + tl.join chain. Table 10 shows the bisected result. Prong B achieved the intended reduction in HBM dependency: long-scoreboard stalls fell from 17.45%17.45\% to 3.33%3.33\%. However, it introduced a stronger SMEM dependency: short-scoreboard stalls rose from 7.04%7.04\% to 15.68%15.68\%. HMMA utilization dropped from 16.6%16.6\% to 10.3%10.3\%, SM throughput fell from 38.5%38.5\% to 26.8%26.8\%, and wall-clock latency regressed by 20%20\% to 0.9520.952 ms, worse than the flex_attention+pre-rotate baseline at 0.8340.834 ms.

Cause and implication.

The root cause is that Triton 3.3.1 lowers the tl.reshape + tl.permute + tl.split + tl.join chain on sm_90 to a SMEM round-trip, not to a register-level warp shuffle. The kernel writes the tile to shared memory, performs the layout permutation there, and reads it back to registers. The SMEM dependency cost exceeds the HBM dependency cost it replaced because Hopper’s L2-cached HBM access for the Krot_halfK_{\text{rot\_half}} load is cheaper than the SMEM staging Triton inserts.

The optimization is right in principle and will pay off as soon as Triton’s lowering recognizes the half-swap pattern as a warp-shuffle candidate. Inline PTX (__shfl_xor_sync) would also achieve the goal but forfeits Triton’s portability. The bisected counter delta in Table 10 provides a falsifiable test case that the Triton compiler community can address. For researchers using Triton, this serves as a cautionary tale: high-level tensor operations on sm_90 may lower to surprising SMEM round-trips that defeat the intended optimization.

8 Related Work

FlashAttention.

Dao et al. [1, 2] pioneered IO-aware tiled attention, establishing the online softmax recurrence and tiled execution that underpin nearly every efficient attention implementation today. AttnFuse adopts the same algorithmic foundation but exposes it through a composable DSL rather than a fixed CUDA binary. FlashAttention-3 [3] is the Hopper-targeted hand-written follow-on; its producer/consumer warp specialization overlaps softmax with the next matmul, recovering some of the non-matmul overhead that limits FA-2 at ∼30%\sim 30\% HMMA on H100 (Section 5). Porting AttnFuse’s codegen to the FA-3 [3] inner-loop structure is a natural next step for closing the residual Hopper gap.

PyTorch flex_attention.

flex_attention (PyTorch 2.5+) is the closest published abstraction to AttnFuse. As discussed in Section 1 and Figure 1, the score_mod hook is post-matmul by design; AttnFuse’s combinator surface includes pre-matmul nodes (rope()) by design. This structural difference is the core distinction: flex_attention is a general-purpose abstraction for modifying scores; AttnFuse is an attention-specific DSL that guarantees single-kernel fusion for any well-formed program, including those with pre-matmul transformations.

Triton and TorchInductor.

Triton [4] provides the JIT compilation infrastructure that both AttnFuse and PyTorch’s TorchInductor build upon. TorchInductor is PyTorch’s Triton-emitting backend for flex_attention and other compiled operations. On Hopper, our investigation (Section 5) finds that TorchInductor’s WGMMA codegen achieves an HMMA pipe ceiling of 32.6%32.6\% at the shape tested. The Rotation Calculus reframes this as a structural property of the FA-2 algorithm rather than a Triton limitation—a finding that has implications for the broader Triton ecosystem. Our documented negative result on Triton 3.3.1’s lowering of reshape/permute chains (Section 7) offers a falsifiable test case for the Triton compiler community.

CUTLASS and vendor libraries.

NVIDIA CUTLASS [12] is a C++ template library for GPU matrix multiplication and attention. PyTorch’s SDPA backend on H100 reaches CUTLASS-class throughput. The matching we report in Section 6.5 (Llama-3-8B forward within 51​μ51\,\mus of SDPA at N=2048N{=}2048) demonstrates how close a high-level DSL can come to hand-tuned vendor libraries—without requiring the developer to write C++ or reason about CUDA specifics.

Domain-specific kernel libraries.

xFormers [13] provides a library of memory-efficient attention kernels but is not a compiler—users choose among hand-written variants. Other libraries such as FlashAttention’s official repository and various open-source implementations offer fixed kernels for common patterns. AttnFuse’s domain-specificity (attention only) is what permits the guaranteed-fusion compiler contract that a general-purpose kernel DSL cannot promise. This narrowness is a feature, not a limitation: it enables the compiler to make strong guarantees about memory behavior and kernel structure.

9 Conclusion and Future Work

We presented AttnFuse, an embedded Python DSL for attention that compiles to fused Triton kernels. The DSL makes RoPE a first-class pre-matmul combinator, offering a strictly more general abstraction than flex_attention’s post-matmul score_mod. On RTX 3090, fused RoPE achieves 2.10×2.10\times over flex_attention. On H100, a tile-swept dispatch path closes 85%85\% of the gap to flex_attention, with tensor-core utilization within 3.23.2 percentage points of the structural ceiling. The Rotation Calculus provides the first systematic quantification of when in-kernel RoPE fusion is profitable as a function of compute-to-bandwidth ratio. End-to-end, AttnFuse runs a Llama-3-8B training step within 5%5\% of hand-tuned SDPA on both architectures.

9.1 Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations point to natural next steps. The Hopper spike currently covers causal MHA/GQA at D∈{64,128}D\in\{64,128\}, fp16/bf16, N≥2048N\geq 2048, forward-only. Extensions include threading cos,sin\cos,\sin through the HuggingFace hook for fused RoPE, widening the spike predicate to LSE-saving forward calls, and extending codegen to sliding-window, ALiBi, and additive-bias variants.

On H100 at N≥8​kN\geq 8\text{k}, pre-rotation wins. Two recovery paths are promising: an FA-3 producer/consumer kernel that overlaps rotation cost with the next matmul, or Triton compiler support for warp-shuffle-lowered half-swap. The negative result we documented provides a concrete test case for the Triton compiler community.

The two-level IR is structurally ready for Ring Attention [10]; lowering to a sequence-parallel kernel would enable scaling across multiple GPUs. Hopper’s fp8 tensor cores offer a natural extension for low-precision training and inference; adding fp8 support introduces one new IR concept.

We believe the Rotation Calculus will outlast the AttnFuse implementation. As accelerators continue to rebalance toward compute, this calculus will become increasingly relevant for AI systems researchers.
